title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (3 of 7)
hook: the eye cannot go there, nor speech, nor the mind
tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (4 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: shrotra; the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind. Your line, the one behind the ear. Did you take one breath behind the listening? Day two hundred forty-one.

Nobody has ever seen their own eyes. A mirror shows a picture of them. The actual eyes, the ones doing the seeing, stay out of sight: the one thing in the field of vision that can never be in the field of vision. A tongue can't taste itself either. The Kena's next verses start from this puzzle. If Brahman is the eye of the eye, then the eye will never see it. And then the text says something that sounds almost shocking for a sacred book.
screen: `NOBODY SEES THEIR OWN EYES.` → `THE ONE THING NEVER IN VIEW.` → `A SHOCKING LINE.`

segments.voice: Verse three: the eye does not go there, nor speech, nor the mind. We don't know it, we don't understand how anyone could teach it. It is other than the known, and beyond the unknown. So we have heard from the ancients who explained it to us. Notice the honesty. The teacher says: we can't hand this to you like an object. Then verses four to eight, five times over, a refrain. That which speech cannot express, but by which speech is expressed: know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here. That which the mind cannot think, but by which the mind thinks. That which the eye cannot see, but by which the eyes see. The ear, the breath, the same. Know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here. What does that line mean? Commentators don't read it as throwing out worship. Hindus go right on worshiping, and the Kena itself will soon tell a story about the gods. The point is sharper: whatever you can set in front of you as an object, even a holy one, is not the one doing the seeing. Shankara reads it that way: Brahman is never an object among objects; it's the subject of all of them. So the image on the altar, the word in the prayer, can point to it. They can't contain it. Vedanta teachers have an old image for this. To show someone the faint star Arundhati, you first point to a bright star beside it. The bright star helps, exactly as long as nobody stops there.
screen: `THE EYE DOES NOT GO THERE.` · `OTHER THAN THE KNOWN, BEYOND THE UNKNOWN.` · `BY WHICH THE EYES SEE.` · `NOT AN OBJECT, THE SEER OF OBJECTS.` · then, large: `KNOW THAT ALONE AS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Open your eyes softly and look at something in front of you. Notice all you can see. Now, without moving your eyes, notice that the seeing is happening from somewhere you can't see. You'll never catch it in view. Close your eyes and do the same with a thought: watch it, and notice you can't turn around and watch the watcher. Don't strain. Just rest in not being able to catch it. The bell holds the time.
Brahman, from brih, to grow, to be great. That which the eye cannot see, but by which the eye sees: know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here.
Your line: the one behind the ear. Today, when you look at something beautiful, remember the one looking is never in the picture. Day two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta often learn the Kena's refrain (1.4–1.8) as a teaching that Brahman is the knower, never an object known, alongside continuing worship of God in images and names.

match.prompt: the Kena's refrain — tap the pairs.

myth: the Kena tells Hindus to stop worshiping
commentators read it as: Brahman is never an object, not as a ban on worship.
the teacher admits he doesn't know how to teach it
verse three: we don't understand how anyone could teach it.
the refrain comes back five times
for speech, mind, eye, ear and breath.

fork.setup: a student asks the teacher to show him Brahman, just once, like an object. what does the Kena say?
options: 'the eye does not go there; it's what the eye sees by.'
fork.reveal: the eye does not go there. Brahman is the one seeing, never one more thing seen.

original.note: Sanskrit: brahman, the ultimate reality; traditionally linked to brih, to grow, to be great.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'not this that people worship' rejects worship.
what it means: nothing you can set in front of you is the one doing the seeing.
what a scholar hears: nedam yad idam upasate; Shankara reads it as Brahman being the subject, never an object (vishaya).
